explanation: Fires on heterogeneous tokens with no shared meaning: second-of-a-pair indices in code (sub2, stamp2), commas in number lists, math operators inside fractions, prepositions and function words in ordinary prose. One faint pattern is a token that repeats or contrasts with an earlier parallel element (sub1/sub2, row1/col1, frogs to foxes / rabbits to robins), but many examples do not fit it.

Fires on assorted content tokens that finish a short noun phrase or idiom (years ago, slam dunk, print archive, animal welfare, Harvard-MIT, TCP), across many topics and code. I can't find one rule that tells strong activations from weak ones.

Fires on the first subword piece of a word the tokenizer splits up, especially rare proper names, foreign-language words and technical terms (transf|obo, Sab|er, nucle|ocapsid, K|GB, f|omepizole, Vir|at, Nak|nek). It fires most when the piece begins a word that has just started and must be continued. Whole common English words fire weakly or not at all.

Fires on a mix of tokens: prepositions and complementizers after a head word (evidenced by, the fact that, unaware of, page of), word-ending suffix pieces (Anklev|ich, incident|ally, posibil|idades), and code punctuation after a method or identifier (getNumber(), log(", println(c). The common thread may be a token that completes a word or phrase begun just before it, but it is loose.

Fires in two settings. In math, it fires on single capital-letter variables in LaTeX (X, U, A), and in code on generic or template openers (Set<T, and_<, {). In English prose, it fires on 'give'/'giving it' and verb-object constructions such as 'give it a shot' or 'make sense'. The two settings don't clearly share an idea.

Fires on characters inside long opaque identifiers or strings: digits and hyphens in GUIDs and UUIDs, hex IDs, URL hashes, timestamps, OIDs, postal codes, grant numbers, format-string placeholders ({4}), and runs of whitespace or tabs. It responds to random-looking alphanumeric sequences, not to ordinary words.

Fires on JSON and schema keys such as "type" and "aws" in config files, on parts of scientific words (MRS, deoxyribonucle|ic, transcobal|amin), and on scattered prose phrase completions (possible, feet, tip of). The examples don't add up to one function.

Fires on a wide mix: medical and anatomical compound pieces (e|jection fraction, intrauter|ine, p|ectoris, partial pressure), code identifiers after a namespace (g:, Video|Mode, table|Output, -p), titles (Miss), and whitespace in legal headers. No common concept is visible.

Fires on the first or middle subword piece of a word the tokenizer fragments, especially rare technical or medical words, place names and foreign words (sup|ram|aximal, cur|tailed, Dec|atur, ter|od|iline, Sch|öne|feld). Whole common words fire weakly. It looks like a word-fragment-continuation unit, similar to U7077.

Fires on tokens that follow a number or quantity (Hz, mg, degrees, 31 of 34), and also on generic function words and nouns in many contexts (the, source, fig, these, second). The quantity-unit part is the clearest, but much of the rest is miscellaneous.

Fires on an abbreviation or acronym written in parentheses right after the full term it stands for, e.g. '(CT)', '(RCT)', '(PEG)', '(GO)', and on pieces of such acronyms. It fires most on the first token inside the opening parenthesis. Acronyms in running text without this definition pattern fire weakly.

Fires at sentence boundaries: on the period or period-plus-newline that ends a sentence or paragraph, and on the first word of the next sentence or a UI-like imperative (Read, Show More, Expand, Support, Based, Establish). It is strongest where a new sentence or segment begins after a completed statement.

Fires most on 'by' in email headers of the form '---- Forwarded by Name/HOU'. It also fires on a scattered set of other tokens (ret|in|oid, plasmin|ogen, run|at, 'common' in 'greatest common factor', '-----Original Message'). The email-header part is clear; the rest is a grab-bag.

Fires on tokens soon after the start of a document or section: just after a title, a heading or an opening line of boilerplate (license texts such as 'list of conditions', '(the "License")', first sentences of Wikipedia-style entries, 'Introduction' sections). The token's identity matters less than its position near the beginning.

Fires in biology and microbiology text near names of organisms, especially taxonomic binomials (Streptoc|occus, Vib|rio, Kibdelosporang|ium). It fires on pieces of those genus names and on prepositions that introduce an organism ('strains of', 'in Arabidopsis', 'by Clostridium'). Outside biological writing it is weak.

Fires on the final subword piece of a geographic place name, such as a region, province, state or city (Sax|ony, Pen|ang, Brand|enburg, Taich|ung, Carmarthens|hire, Fuku|oka, Val|ais). Single-token, well-known places like Montreal or Cleveland fire only moderately or weakly.

Fires on words that introduce a list of examples: 'such as' (on 'as'), 'including', 'namely', 'include' (e.g. 'Notable people with the surname include'), 'the first describes'. 'like' and 'For example,' fire moderately.

Fires on sports text, especially the sport word in biographical descriptions ('is a Japanese football player', 'American soccer player', 'Tonga rugby league'). It also fires moderately on function words in sports news about clubs, players and managers. It is strongest on 'football'/'soccer' following a nationality.

Fires in code on member-access and method-chaining punctuation, i.e. the token right after a call or cast closes and before the next member is accessed ('().', ').', '->', '").', ' .'). It also fires on type or keyword tokens after 'public' in Java or C#. A few non-code word fragments also fire.

Fires on an opening square bracket '[' in almost any context, such as citation brackets '\[[@B1]', isotope labels '[3H]', chemical complexes '[Mn', array indexing, markdown links, and regex character classes. A preceding space or backslash makes it strongest. Closing brackets fire only weakly.

Fires mostly on adverbs that modify a following verb or adjective in formal prose (effectively, adversely, partially, adequately, significantly, further, individually). It also fires on scattered other tokens, such as surname particles (Van, Yan) and pronouns starting a clause. The adverb pattern dominates, with miscellaneous extras.
